To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
magnesium, calcium and hydrogen ion each can influence the interaction of calcium crystals with renal cells.

magnesium and calcium, in supraphysiologically high concentrations, can block the adhesion of calcium oxalates to renal epithelial cells, and that this is mediated by the effect of these ions on the surface properties of the crystals.
magnesium, calcium and hydrogen ion each influence the efficiency of calcium crystal interactions with cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of magnesium, calcium, and hydrogen ions in the adhesion of calcium oxalates to renal cells, which is a key event in the development of calcium oxalosis and nephrolithiasis.
the effect of calcium, magnesium and hydrogen ion concentration on the surface of calcium-containing stones.
the role of ions in the interaction between calcium oxalate and renal epithelial cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of magnesium in the urine, in the form of a magnesium-containing crystal, is unlikely to be a significant contributor to the formation of kidney stones.
the surface of calcium crystals is a dynamic, ever changing entity, which can be modified by the presence of ions in the solution.
the presence of magnesium and calcium ions at the crystal surface can have a profound impact on the adhesion of preformed calcium oxalate to cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface of the calcium oxalate stone is a dynamic entity, and that the physiologic milieu can exert profound effects on its structure, composition, and function.
magnesium, calcium, and hydrogen ions each influence crystal-cell interactions in a concentration-dependent manner.
magnesium, calcium and pH all play an important role during cell-crystal interactions and, therefore, may be important in the pathogenesis of renal stone formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the interaction of calcium and magnesium with renal cell surface molecules is a dynamic process which is influenced by both the ambient concentration of these two ions as well as by the local charge distribution on the crystal surface.
the surface chemistry of calcium oxalates can be modified by the presence of other cations and anions, and this may be important in the pathogenesis of renal stones.
the physiologic environment can have an important influence on the interaction of calcium-containing stones with renal cells.
